meta.title: Who really said "Children today are lazy and disrespectful"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Socrates. The passage is a paraphrase written by Kenneth John Freeman for his 1907 Cambridge dissertation 'Schools of Hellas' — his own summary of ancient complaints about the young. A newspaper pinned it on Socrates in 1922 and it never came off.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Children today are lazy and disrespectful'?
meta.ogDescription: It is a 1907 Cambridge dissertation, not a Greek philosopher. Kenneth John Freeman summarised ancient grumbles about youth; the Oakland Tribune handed the summary to Socrates in 1922.

answer.label: Not Socrates — a 1907 dissertation paraphrase
answer.authorDates: d. 1906 · Cambridge classicist · Schools of Hellas, published 1907
answer.sourceLine: Socrates wrote nothing. Everything we have of him comes through Plato, Xenophon, Aristophanes or Diogenes Laërtius — and this passage is in none of them. What actually happened is that a young Cambridge classicist, Kenneth John Freeman, wrote a dissertation called Schools of Hellas (published 1907) in which he summarised in his own words the standard ancient complaints about young people. He never claimed to be quoting anybody. By 1922 an American newspaper was printing his summary as Socrates, and it has been travelling under that name ever since.
answer.confidenceText: The grumble is genuinely ancient. The sentence is Edwardian.

source.excerpt: The counts of the indictment are luxury, bad manners, contempt for authority, disrespect to elders, and a love for chatter in place of exercise.
trail: Socrates wrote nothing, so everything we have of him is second-hand — chiefly through Plato, Xenophon, Aristophanes and later compilers such as Diogenes Laërtius. This passage appears in none of the ancient sources, in any wording, in any translation.

It is in Freeman. On p. 74 of Schools of Hellas he writes his own résumé of the ancient case against the young — ‘luxury, bad manners, contempt for authority, disrespect to elders, and a love for chatter in place of exercise’ — and a few lines later adds that children ‘no longer rose from their seats when an elder entered the room; they contradicted their parents, chattered before company, gobbled up the dainties at table.’ The recognisable phrases of the best-known ‘Socrates’ version are all there, in an Edwardian Englishman’s prose; the wording on this page is a later, looser rewrite of it the tracing ↗.

The handover is datable. In 1912 the educator James J. Walsh quoted the passage and correctly credited Freeman. By 1922 the Oakland Tribune was running it as Socrates, and that is the version the twentieth century inherited. The Library of Congress’s Respectfully Quoted (1989), compiled from Congressional Research Service enquiries, reached the same verdict in one word: spurious.
source.excerptNote: Freeman’s actual sentence. Read it as what it is — a scholar listing, in his own words, the charges Greek writers levelled at the young. There are no quotation marks around it in the original because it is not a quotation of anyone.
source.rightsNote: Freeman’s Schools of Hellas was published posthumously in 1907; Freeman himself died in 1906, so the text is public domain worldwide and free to quote. The ancient material Freeman was summarising — Aristophanes’ Clouds and the rest — is likewise out of copyright in the original Greek, though a specific modern translation of it may not be. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Socrates
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Socrates
author.bio: Socrates is the ideal host for a fake quotation because there is no manuscript to check him against — he wrote not a word, and everything attributed to him is already second-hand through Plato, Xenophon, Aristophanes or Diogenes Laërtius. He was also, famously, prosecuted for corrupting the young men of Athens, which makes a grumble about badly behaved teenagers feel like it belongs to him. It is exactly backwards: at his trial he was cast as the one doing the corrupting, not the one complaining about it.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is probably the most-repeated fake classical quotation in existence, and the reason it survives is that it is almost true — the sentiment really is ancient, so nobody feels a jolt when they read it.

items.why: Socrates wrote nothing, so everything attributed to him comes second-hand — chiefly through Plato, Xenophon, Aristophanes and later compilers such as Diogenes Laërtius. This passage is in none of the ancient sources: no manuscript, no fragment, no ancient testimony — nothing to argue about.

Freeman’s dissertation summarised the ancient complaints in his own words: ‘luxury, bad manners, contempt for authority, disrespect to elders, and a love for chatter in place of exercise.’ He set no quotation marks around it, because he was not quoting anybody the trail ↗.

A comparable rant about slack, disrespectful youths really does appear in Aristophanes’ Clouds — but it is delivered by the character of Just Discourse, and in that same play Socrates is the satirical target, not the moralist.

Republic 563a–b really does describe the young in a democracy despising their teachers — and it is one of the three passages (with Aristophanes’ Clouds and Isocrates’ Areopagiticus) that Freeman was summarising on p. 74. But it is spoken by Socrates as a character in Plato’s dialogue, not reported as a saying of his, and its wording is not the sentence on this page.

‘Lazy and disrespectful,’ ‘children are now tyrants,’ ‘they gobble their food’ — the versions in circulation have been rewritten repeatedly over a century. None of the wordings matches any ancient text, and most no longer match Freeman either.

misattribution.truthLine: Kenneth John Freeman’s own summary of ancient complaints, written for a Cambridge dissertation published in 1907 and handed to Socrates by an American newspaper in 1922 the tracing ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The quotation is loved because of what it appears to prove: that every generation has said this, so your own irritation with teenagers is a permanent feature of human nature rather than a sign that you are getting old. That is a genuinely comforting thought, which is why nobody checks it.

The joke turns out to be doubled. The sentiment really is 2,400 years old — you can find versions of it in Greek comedy — but the sentence people quote to prove it is a hundred-odd years old and English. The evidence is fake; the phenomenon it is offered as evidence for is real.
context.detailsSummary: The main places a Socrates quote could be
detailsBody: Plato — the dialogues, where Socrates is the central speaker. Nothing resembling this.
Xenophon — the Memorabilia and related works, a soldier’s plainer portrait of the same man. Nothing.
Aristophanes — the Clouds, a hostile comic caricature written in Socrates’ lifetime. Contains a similar grumble, but from a different character, and aimed partly at Socrates.
Diogenes Laërtius — the third-century AD compiler who collected the philosophers’ sayings and quips. Nothing.
These are the main witnesses, not the only ones — later writers such as Aristotle and Plutarch also transmit Socratic material — but this passage is in none of them either.
context.pull: The sentiment is 2,400 years old. The sentence is from 1907.
